accroche: The Sahara always comes first when people name the world's largest desert. It actually ranks third, far behind a continent of ice.
contenu_vulgarise:
Ask someone to name the world's largest desert: the Sahara almost always comes first, with its dunes, heat, and camels. Yet it is not the largest desert on the planet, and not by a long shot: that title belongs to a continent entirely covered in ice.

## The Mechanism

The confusion lies in the word itself. A desert is defined not by heat but by dryness: by the commonly used threshold, any region receiving less than 250 mm of precipitation a year (rain, snow, or fog, whatever the form) falls into the category. Nothing in that definition requires sand or a high thermometer reading.

Yet Antarctica receives, on average across the whole continent, the equivalent of about 150 mm of water a year, almost entirely as snow. The internal contrast is sharp: the interior of the polar plateau, the coldest and driest part, receives only about 50 mm a year (the air there is so cold that it barely holds enough water vapor to condense any), while the milder coastal belt can receive up to 500 mm. Even the continental average stays well below the threshold of the classic hot deserts.

On the scale of surface area, the ranking leaves no doubt: the Antarctic desert covers about 14.2 million km², against 9.2 million for the Sahara, a gap of nearly 5 million km².

## The Shift

What flips is not just a schoolbook geography record, it is the mental image attached to the word “desert.” We spontaneously associate it with excess: too much heat, too little life; the scientific definition retains only a deficit, that of water falling from the sky. A continent can thus be built on kilometers of ice accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years (the trace not of an excess of water, but of snow that fell in tiny quantities and never melted) and remain, climatically, the most arid of all: Antarctica is described, in the scientific literature devoted to it, as the coldest, driest, and windiest of the continents. The Sahara, by contrast, loses each night a good share of the heat it stores by day, and remains in that sense one “hot” desert among others: a subgenus, whereas Antarctica occupies the entire category by size alone.

carte.punch: Antarctica, a desert of 14.2 million km² against 9.2 for the Sahara, has neither sand nor heat.
carte.idee: A desert is defined by lack of rain, not by heat: less than 250 mm a year. Antarctica receives about 150 mm on average, 50 mm in the interior. By surface area: 14.2 million km² of desert, against 9.2 million for the Sahara.

quiz.question: Why is Antarctica considered the world's largest desert?
choix: Because it is the largest landmass entirely covered by a single type of climate
Because a desert is defined by low precipitation, not by temperature, and Antarctica receives less than the Sahara
Because no plant or animal life survives there, which is enough to classify it as a desert
Because all poles are considered deserts by definition, regardless of measured rainfall
quiz.explication: A desert is classified by its precipitation deficit (less than 250 mm a year), not by its heat or its lack of life. Antarctica, far below that threshold over most of its surface, thus becomes the world's largest desert by area, far ahead of the Sahara.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What annual precipitation threshold is used to define a desert, according to the card?
choix: Less than 50 mm a year, only as snow
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card uses a threshold of 250 mm of annual precipitation, rain, snow, and fog combined, with no condition tied to the temperature of the place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the scientific literature cited on the card describe the Antarctic continent?
choix: As the hottest and wettest of the continents
As the coldest, driest, and windiest of the continents
As the continent richest in plant biodiversity
As a continent with a climate comparable to that of the Sahara
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card cites the scientific literature that describes Antarctica as the coldest, driest, and windiest of the continents, despite its immense ice cover.
